title: Go Generics at Package Boundaries: Type Parameter Leakage, Interface Erosion, and the Constraint Design Problem
description: How generic type parameters escape package boundaries, erode interface contracts, and what constraint design choices cost you in real service APIs.
linkedin_post:
Go generics are genuinely useful inside a package. Across a package boundary—into a shared SDK, an internal library, or a service API—they introduce a class of problems that aren't obvious until you're debugging a cascade of compilation failures across 15 microservices.

The core issue: type parameters are not abstracted away at the boundary. They're exported. Every downstream consumer must now carry that type variable, instantiate it, wire it, and handle the constraint requirements you chose when you wrote the library. If you chose `any`, you pushed the entire safety problem onto callers. If you chose a structural constraint, you've made every future model change a potential breaking change.

My latest article works through the specific mechanics:

→ Why `Repository[T any]` becomes a maintenance liability when composed across services
→ The pointer receiver problem in constrained generics (and why `Get` panics in ways your tests miss)
→ Why reflection, mock generators, and structured loggers degrade silently with generic types
→ The three rules that govern when and how generic types should cross package boundaries
→ A five-question decision framework before you export a type parameter

The conclusion isn't "avoid generics." It's that instantiation belongs at the boundary, and the concrete type—not the generic template—is what your API consumers should ever see.

If you're designing shared libraries, internal SDKs, or service-layer abstractions in Go, this is the design pressure that matters most right now.
